newsitem.title: CHINA: China moves to tighten grip on state media.
newsitem.headline: China moves to tighten grip on state media.

text.p: China's Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin moved on Friday to tighten the communists' grip on the state media and to strengthen his position with a blaze of publicity before a party plenum.

He used a visit to the Beijing offices of the People's Daily, the party mouthpiece, to deliver a hardline speech on the importance of maintaining communist control of all media, the newspaper reported, splashing the news and three photographs of Jiang across its front page.

Diplomats said the speech by Jiang was aimed at bringing back into line Chinese writers and more daring media organisations that have tried to push the limits of propaganda restrictions over the past two years.

State television devoted most of its main evening news broadcast on Thursday to showing Jiang's People's Daily tour, his third highly publicised appearance this week, and diplomats said the party chief and designated heir to paramount leader Deng Xiaoping appeared to be trying to shore up his position.

The party is expected to hold its annual plenum early next month. Jiang will need to muster all his political forces to demonstrate he is in control and to fight off opposition to his leadership and policies from within the highly secretive Politburo and Central Committee.
"The leadership of the media should be in the firm grip of people loyal to Marxism, loyal to the party and loyal to the people," the People's Daily quoted Jiang as saying.
Jiang followed the lead of late Chairman Mao Zedong by underlining the importance of the state-controlled propaganda machine to continued Communist Party rule in China.
"Media work can be said to be ideological work," Jiang said. "It is related to the future and the fate of the party and the state. Party news organisations are a part of the very life of the party."
He reminded Chinese media that their role was to provide ideological underpinning for Communist Party rule and to stir up the people in support of the party.

"Historical experience has proved repeatedly that whether guidance of news is right or wrong has to do with the party growing strong ... the solidarity of the people and the prosperity of the nation," Jiang said.
"If the direction of ideology is correct, this is a blessing for the party and the people, but if the direction of ideology is incorrect, this is a disaster for the party and the people."

Diplomats said Jiang's speech was the latest sign of a freeze across China's cultural world. China's propaganda tsars have asserted their authority in recent weeks by removing the president of the most outspoken newspaper in China's capital. It had reported a poisoning case that was alleged to have caused a plunge in sales of a state-owned beverage manufacturer.
Cui Enqing was sacked as president of the the Beijing Youth Daily and replaced by Chen Xing, a deputy editor-in-chief of the rival and conservative Beijing Daily, on September 17.

The Beijing Youth Daily had become the city's most popular newspaper, on sale at most streetside stalls. It had unusually open coverage of disasters and a sensational approach to news compared with the stultifying diet of good news and party propaganda offered up by other newspapers.
